activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: The Gunnery camp, begun in 1861 by Connecticut schoolmaster Frederick W. Gunn, who led his students on a hike to a camp by the sea, is usually considered the first organized American summer camp.
story:
Elliot had claimed the bunk by the window before anyone else could drop a duffel bag on it, because a window bunk was the best one in Cabin Four, and he intended to cherish it for the next two weeks. His dad had driven him three hours into the hills that morning, and now the cabin smelled like pine and somebody's strawberry shampoo. Across the room, a kid named Jude was trying to force a sleeping bag into a bag that was clearly too small, and a girl named Angie was taping a photo of a dog above her bunk even though this was a boys' cabin and she had wandered in by mistake.

"Wrong cabin," Elliot said, grinning. "Unless the dog needs a bunk too."

"I'm reading the plaque on your wall," Angie said, pointing above the window. "You didn't even notice it, and it's right next to your head."

The plaque was small and the print was sparse, just a few lines of old bronze lettering. Elliot leaned close. He had assumed summer camps were a pretty new thing, something his grandparents' generation invented, maybe. But the plaque said this camp's whole tradition went back to the Gunnery camp, begun in 1861 by a Connecticut schoolmaster named Frederick W. Gunn, who led his students on a hike to a camp by the sea, and that it was usually considered the first organized American summer camp. A hundred and sixty years of campers before him. He read it twice.

Jude gave up on the sleeping bag and came over. "Nobody had camp before that?" he said. "Nobody ever thought, hey, let's sleep outside for fun?"

Elliot considered it. "Maybe they camped, but not organized. Like, this place has schedules and counselors and a dining hall. That's the difference." It made sense to him, the way a rule makes sense once you see it: the idea wasn't the woods, the idea was doing it on purpose, together.

Then Mr. Diallo, the counselor, rapped on the doorframe and announced the first hike of the session left in twenty minutes, and Elliot faced a genuine dilemma. His stomach had been sour since the parking lot, and he'd been planning to claim he felt sick and stay behind to unpack slowly and maybe not do anything hard all day. Jude was clearly nervous too, because he suddenly became very interested in reorganizing his bag. But a kid from 1861 had hiked all the way to the sea with his schoolmaster, without bug spray or a water bottle with a carrying strap, and that kid had started the whole thing.

"Twenty minutes," Elliot said, and pulled his boots on. "You coming or reorganizing forever?"

Jude looked at the bag, then at the door, then grabbed his own boots. "Coming. First one to the trailhead picks the pace."

"Deal," said Elliot, and he was already out the door, taking the porch steps two at a time, with Angie's voice behind him shouting, "Wait, I want to see the plaque after!"

activity: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
knowledge_domain: to build a debate case with a claim, evidence and a warrant for each point
fact: A straw man argument misstates an opponent's position as something weaker or sillier, then attacks that version instead of the real one.
story:
The community theatre smelled like dust and old velvet, and Nevaeh spread her debate notes across the stage floor under the ghost light. She was supposed to argue that the school day should have a shorter lunch period, with ten extra minutes moved to afternoon classes, and she had spent three days collecting evidence: a survey of sixty students, an article about afternoon focus, a quote from a teacher. But something was wrong and she couldn't name it.

Alessandra arrived with her backpack slung over one shoulder and dropped down beside the notes. "You look like your case is a leaky boat," she said.

"It's porous," Nevaeh admitted, touching the pages. "The points just don't hold together." She remembered the practice round last week, when she had stacked up fact after fact and Ms. Tran had only said, "So what? Why does this prove your claim?" Nevaeh had shrugged, and the round had collapsed like a wave retreating down a beach.

Desmond, who was on the other side of the practice debate, paced across the stage. "Ready to lose?" he called. When the round started, he stood at the front and pointed at Nevaeh. "My opponent wants to cut lunch down to almost nothing, so students would basically have no break at all. Is that fair? No recess ever, no time to eat, no rest."

Nevaeh opened her mouth to defend herself, then stopped. That wasn't her position. She had never said anything like that. She flipped through her notes, found her claim written at the top in her own handwriting, and stood up slowly. "That's not what I said," she replied. "I said ten minutes. You changed my position into something sillier and then attacked that instead."

"That's called a straw man," Alessandra said from the front row.

Desmond's ears went red. "Fine, fine," he muttered, and started over, this time quoting Nevaeh's actual claim. When he did, she suddenly saw what her case had been missing. Each of her points needed a bridge, a sentence that carried the evidence to the claim, the way a warrant carries a ticket to a seat. She scribbled beside her survey: students who feel drowsy by two o'clock lose focus, and moving ten minutes restores it, therefore afternoon classes improve. The pieces clicked.

They ran the round again in the empty theatre, voices bouncing off the balcony. Nevaeh inhaled before her final speech, feeling the argument hold its shape all the way through. Desmond shook her hand at the end, and she looked down at her notes, one bridge at a time, still deciding whether the second warrant really carried the weight she'd put on it. "Same time tomorrow?" he asked, already gathering his cards.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: In the United States, the USDA says a 'best if used by' date shows when a food will be at its best quality; it is not a food-safety date.
story:
Mason had never been inside the community garden's tool shed before Saturday, but that was where the food bank had set up its sorting table, right between the raspberry beds and the compost bins. Diana waved him over and handed him a clipboard. "You write down what comes in," she said. "London weighs it. I sort." She paused. "Actually, Mason, I'll delegate the clipboard to you and take sorting myself, since I've done it twice before." A woman from the garden's steering committee, Ms. Ortiz, rolled a crate of donations from the parking lot, and the three of them got to work.

The crate held canned beans, pasta, rice, and six boxes of cereal. London weighed everything and called out numbers while Mason logged them, and for twenty minutes it went smoothly. Then Diana picked up a cereal box, frowned at the date printed near the top flap, and dropped it into the discard bin. The next box got the same treatment. By the fourth box, Mason put down his clipboard.

"Why are those going out?" he asked.

"Past their date," Diana said. "You can't hand out expired food."

Mason pulled one from the bin and turned it over in his hands. The date was only one day past. That seemed strange to him. If a food actually became unsafe, wouldn't the danger build up over weeks, not flip on overnight like a light switch? He noticed the boxes didn't say "expired" or "use by" anywhere. They said something else, in small curly letters: best if used by. Was that the same thing as a rule about throwing food out, or was it more like advice? And if it was advice, advice about what?

"Ms. Ortiz," he called across the shed, "can I use the office computer for a second?" She nodded, and he looked up the phrase on the USDA's website. What he found made him grin. He came back holding his phone like evidence. "These aren't safety dates," he told Diana. "In the United States, the USDA says a 'best if used by' date shows when a food will be at its best quality. It's not a food-safety date." Diana read the screen herself, slowly, then pulled all four boxes back out of the discard bin and set them on the keep shelf.

At the end of the afternoon, Ms. Ortiz tallied the numbers on the whiteboard. "Nice work," she said. "And because of Mason, our discard pile is about half the size it was last month, which means the percentage of usable food going out to families just went up." She pointed her marker at the whiteboard. "Ask questions like that every week." Mason looked at the six cereal boxes stacked on the keep shelf, then at the discard bin, which now held only a torn bag of flour and one dented can. He picked up the clipboard for the next crate. "So what's the rule for dented cans?" he asked. Diana laughed. "One mystery at a time."

activity: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
knowledge_domain: to describe how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands
fact: Beak size is inherited, so after the 1977 drought the survivors' offspring had larger beaks on average than the birds before the drought.
story:
Lucas stared at the worksheet on the kitchen table and tapped his pencil against the edge of his glass. "Explain how natural selection changed the beak shapes of finches on different islands," he read aloud for the third time. His mom had enrolled him in the advanced science elective two weeks ago, and this was the first assignment that made him feel like the whole class might have been a mistake. He had notes, half a page of them, and no idea how to turn them into an answer.

His phone buzzed. It was Wassim, calling from down the street. "Are you stuck too?" Wassim asked before Lucas even said hello.

"Totally stuck," Lucas admitted. "I get that the finches on the different islands have different beaks. What I don't get is how it happened. Nobody was there watching it."

"Maybe you just write that it's a mystery," Wassim said, and Lucas could hear him eating something. "The teacher can't expect us to know what nobody saw."

Lucas hung up, but the idea bothered him instead of comforting him. He flipped through the packet Mr. Whitehead had handed out and stopped at a page he'd skipped, a chart with columns of measurements. One column was labeled before 1977, and one was labeled after. The numbers after were bigger, but bigger for what, he didn't know yet, because the top of the page was smudged where his water glass had sat. His fatigue from soccer practice made the rows swim, and he almost shoved the whole packet aside.

Then he found the paragraph on the back, and it named the thing he couldn't see. In 1977, a drought had hit the island. Only some birds survived. He looked again at the chart and realized what it measured: beak size. The survivors passed their beaks on, because beak size is inherited. He checked the two columns again, slowly, tracing each row with his finger. The birds after the drought, the survivors' offspring, had larger beaks on average than the birds before the drought. The change had happened between generations, invisible while it was happening, the way nobody watches a family nose get passed down until you line up the photographs.

Lucas grabbed his phone and called Wassim back. "It's not a mystery," he said. "The beaks got bigger after a drought in 1977, on average, because the survivors passed them down. It's probable the same thing happened on the other islands, just with different food. I can prove it with the chart." He turned the packet over, smoothed the smudged page flat, and started to write.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: During the fight-or-flight response, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, which makes the heart beat faster and breathing speed up.
story:
Nicholas sat on his bedroom floor with his flashcards spread around him like a paper moat. Tomorrow he had to give the mandatory five-minute science talk in Mr. Littlechild's class, and even though he had practiced eleven times, his heart was hammering as if he were being chased. He pressed two fingers to his wrist and counted. Way too fast. "Nothing is even happening," he said out loud, and his own voice sounded strange in the empty room.

He pulled his mom's nursing textbook from under his bed, the one she used for her night classes, and flipped until he found the chapter on stress. There it was, a diagram with an arrow. When the body switches into fight-or-flight mode, the adrenal glands release adrenaline, and adrenaline makes the heart beat faster and speeds up breathing. So that was the hidden cause. His brain had classified tomorrow's presentation as a danger, same as a bear, even though no bear had ever assigned homework. His body was reacting to something he could only see the results of: the pounding, the quick breath, the sweaty palms.

He tested it. If the adrenaline was the cause, then slow breathing should be the lever. He set a timer for one minute and breathed in for four counts, out for six, the coping trick Makayla had shown him after the last test. His pulse crept down. He tried again. Down again. It was like finding the right wire to cut, except the wire was invisible and the wire was him.

His phone buzzed. Makayla's face filled the screen, her own flashcards held up to the camera. "Did you finish slide six? Because I rewrote mine twice." She paused and squinted. "You look weird. Are you nervous?"

"Sort of, but I figured something out," Nicholas said. "My heart pounds because of adrenaline. Fight-or-flight. It's like my body has a smoke alarm, but the sensor can't tell a bear from a book report." He showed her the diagram. "Slow breathing actually works. I timed it."

Makayla grinned. "Okay, boundary time, though. I'm hanging up at nine, because staying up till midnight makes my anxiety ten times worse, and I'm being strict about it."

"Fair," Nicholas said. "Night."

The next morning he stood beside Mr. Littlechild's desk, lungs doing the four-and-six count, and the twist came before he said a single word. "Nicholas, good news," Mr. Littlechild announced to the whole class. "The fire drill yesterday knocked the schedule sideways, so presentations are now Thursday instead of today." A wave of groans went around the room, but Nicholas laughed. His heart had hammered for a danger that wasn't even on the right day. He sat down, placed his flashcards neatly in order, and thought: Thursday, heart, hammer. I know exactly which wire to cut.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Two players can have the same average while one is steady and the other swings between great and terrible games, since an average hides how spread out the results are.
story:
Autumn spread the two scoring sheets across the dinner table, moving her plate of rice to the side before her mother could complain. The tournament roster was due by nine o'clock tomorrow morning, and she had exactly one open spot. Miley leaned over her shoulder while Ms. Ndlovu, their neighbour who had come over for dinner, buttered a roll and watched.

"Octavia and Dana," Miley said, tapping the papers. "Both average twelve points a game. It's a tie. Just flip a coin."

But Autumn didn't like coin flips. She pulled the sheets closer and began to read the game-by-game column, the one nobody ever looked at because the average was printed at the bottom in bold. Octavia's games went twelve, eleven, twelve, thirteen, twelve. Dana's went twenty-six, two, twenty-one, zero, eleven. Autumn checked the bold numbers again. Both said the same thing. She turned the pages over, as if the backs might tell her something different.

"There's the average, and then there's this," she said slowly, tapping the long column. "Same average, but look how Octavia's numbers sit together, and Dana's jump all over. One of them you can plan around tomorrow, and one you can't." She went quiet, working it through. "If we pick Dana, we either get a superstar or we get nothing. If we pick Octavia, we know what we're getting." Miley shook her head, still certain the coin flip made more sense, and went to refill her water just to get away from the papers.

The kitchen had gone tranquil except for the hum of the fridge. Ms. Ndlovu set down her fork. "When I was a girl," she said, "my grandfather would say an emperor who only ever heard one number about his whole kingdom knew nothing about his kingdom." She smiled and went back to her rice, offering nothing more.

Autumn stared at the two columns. Then she grabbed a pencil and tried a small test right there on a napkin. She wrote out what the team would need tomorrow, about eleven points from the open spot to be safe, and she imagined each sheet as tomorrow's game. With Octavia, the napkin math held together. With Dana, the total swung from brilliant to nowhere. She imagined trying to integrate a player like that into a game plan, every play a gamble.

Miley came back and looked over her shoulder at the napkin. "Okay," she said, after a long minute. "Okay, I get it now. Call Octavia."

Autawn reached for her phone on the table, and her thumb hovered over Octavia's name as the clock in the hallway struck eight.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: A baking soda volcano erupts because baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) reacts with vinegar (acetic acid) to produce carbon dioxide gas.
story:
Emma spread her notes across the library table and pressed down the corner that kept curling. Her volcano was due at the science fair in three days, and everyone in her class would build the same brown cone that oozed foam once and stopped. She wanted hers to actually show something.

"Move over," said Emanuel, dropping his backpack beside her. He was building a volcano too, but bigger, with a plastic bottle inside and a plan he would not stop talking about. "Mine's going to erupt for a whole minute. I just don't know how to make it bigger without making a mess."

Emma tapped her pencil on her data sheet. "It's the bubbles," she said. "The foam is just bubbles being pushed up. More bubbles, bigger eruption."

"Where do the bubbles come from, though?"

"That's what I'm trying to figure out." She had watched hers erupt a dozen times in the garage, but watching wasn't the same as knowing. She'd tried more baking soda once and nothing changed, which meant the baking soda probably wasn't the thing that ran out. So she had drawn four boxes on her sheet and labeled them with different amounts of vinegar.

"You measured vinegar," Emanuel said, reading over her shoulder. He looked hesitant, like he wasn't sure he wanted to hear the answer. "Because if it turns out the amount doesn't matter, my whole minute-long plan falls apart."

"Then we test it," Emma said. "Here. Now."

They couldn't erupt volcanoes in the library, so they used what they had: baking soda from Emanuel's backpack, four paper cups, and vinegar from the little bottle Emma kept for exactly this kind of emergency. She put one spoonful of baking soda in each cup and poured a different amount of vinegar into each one, counting under her breath. In the first cup, with barely a splash, the fizz rose and died fast. The second cup did better. The third and fourth cups, with the most vinegar, overflowed onto the table in white foam that smelled like salad dressing.

"Get paper towels," Emma whispered, but she was grinning. She wrote her numbers down while the cups still hissed. The more vinegar, the more gas, and the gas was what did the pushing.

Mr. Wanjiru appeared with the paper towels before Emanuel got back. He mopped the puddle without a word about the smell, then nodded at her data sheet. "You're going to advocate for measuring at the fair, aren't you," he said. "Nobody ever does."

At the fair, while the other volcanoes fizzled in single sad burps, Emma set out her cups in a line and let the judges watch the eruption climb from small to huge. A boy in the second row leaned forward and read her chart out loud, and behind him, Emanuel's volcano foamed for fifty-eight seconds.

"Two more seconds," Emma said, and wrote it down.

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: Robert Hooke named cells in his 1665 book Micrographia after seeing tiny compartments in a thin slice of cork under his microscope.
story:
Aurora slipped the onion slide under the clips and bent toward the eyepiece, holding her breath the way you do when you are afraid your own shaking will ruin everything. The lab sheet said to label three things: the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus. She could see the walls easily, brick-shaped boxes fitted together like a honeycomb. But everything inside them was a pale smear, and her worksheet was still blank.

"Find yours yet?" Courtney whispered from the next stool.

"Not the nucleus." Aurora turned the fine focus a hair at a time. The image sharpened, then swam out again, and something small and dark floated up in one cell and sank away before she could be sure of it. She gripped the edge of the table. Mr. Do had said there would be no second slides until everyone had a first attempt drawn, and the drawing was worth half the lab grade, which counted toward a cumulative score for the whole museum unit. One bad day could drag weeks of work down with it.

"Try less light," Alejandro offered. "I did and it helped."

She dialed the mirror down. That was when the dark spot came back, a round dot near the middle of one cell, sitting quietly as a stone at the bottom of a pond. The nucleus. She began to sketch, but her eyes kept snagging on the walls. There was something familiar about those boxes, something she had seen that morning and could not place. The feeling itched at her all through the drawing.

Then she remembered. On the way in, past the gift shop, there was a glass case the museum kept dark to conserve the old things inside it. She had glanced at it for maybe three seconds. She set her pencil down. "Stay with my scope," she told Courtney, and hurried back through the hall, sneakers squeaking on the polished floor.

The case held an open book under dim light. The label read Micrographia, 1665, by Robert Hooke, and beside it a large printed drawing of cork. Aurora leaned close. Tiny compartments, row after row, box beside box, exactly the way her onion cells looked under the lens. She read the caption twice. Robert Hooke named cells in his 1665 book Micrographia after seeing tiny compartments in a thin slice of cork under his microscope. Cells. The word on her worksheet had a history, and it started with someone staring at cork three hundred and fifty years ago.

She ran back to the lab, slid onto her stool, and checked that the spot was still there. It was, patient and dark. "He called them cells," she said, mostly to herself, but Alejandro heard.

"Who did?"

"Robert Hooke. His book is right down the hall, and his cork drawing looks like my slide." She labeled the nucleus, then the wall, then drew the thin line just inside it and wrote membrane. Mr. Do walked by and paused at her page.

"Nice work," he said. "You even put the membrane where it belongs."

Aurora smiled and looked back into the eyepiece at the little boxes Hooke had named.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: iPhones and Android phones let you choose, app by app, whether an app may use your location always, only while you are using it, or never.
story:
Alicia was still holding her phone when the group chat buzzed for the fourth time. Someone with the username hawk_474 had joined mid-conversation, right after Angelique posted a picture of the three of them on Angelique's front steps, and hawk_474 had written, "nice house on Delmore, the one with the blue door." Alicia read it twice. The blue door was Angelique's. Only the chat members were supposed to see that photo, and none of them went by hawk_474.

"I'm deleting it," Angelique typed, and the photo vanished from the thread, but the worry didn't vanish with it. Alicia tried to classify what had happened. Either someone in the chat had forwarded the picture, or something on their phones had told a stranger where they were. She stared at the little arrow icon beside the message and thought about all the apps she'd installed over the past year, the games and filters and quiz apps, each one she'd tapped through quickly on setup day.

The next morning in the school computer lab, she slid into the seat beside Randy and put her phone on the desk between them. "Somebody knew Angelique's street from a photo," she said. "Can you help me figure out if it's my phone?"

Randy picked up the phone and started tapping through settings, quiet and unhurried the way he was in science class. "Okay, so here," he said, turning the screen toward her. "You can pick, for each app, whether it may use your location always, only while you're using it, or never." He scrolled down the list. A geography quiz app she'd used twice last fall said Always. A flashlight app said Always. The game she played on the bus, the one where the screen camouflage matched whatever room you were in, said Always too.

"That game doesn't need to know where I am," Alicia said. She tapped Never on all three, one after another, and felt something settle, like closing a window at night. It was subjective, maybe, how much it mattered, but it mattered to her. "Angelique's going to do this too. And I'm going to ask the group chat to."

"Ask them what happened to hawk_474," Randy said.

She typed the message right there, leaning over the keyboard under the lab's humming lights: "Everyone check your location settings. All three choices, app by app." Then she opened the chat settings and removed hawk_474, and the little gray arrow icon beside the stranger's name finally went gray and stayed gray.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: On a standard 400-metre outdoor track, the 800 metres is exactly two laps, so runners plan the race as a first lap and a second lap.
story:
Natalie stood at the edge of the baseball diamond, where the outfield fence had been pushed back and chalk lines made a rough oval in the grass. Mr. Hosseini had measured it the night before with a long tape and marked the corners with orange cones. "Four hundred metres around," he said. "Same as a real track." He clapped his hands. "Eight hundred metres is exactly two laps, so you plan the race as a first lap and a second lap. First lap controlled, second lap everything you have left."

That was the part Natalie could not do. Every time she ran the eight hundred, she sprinted the first lap like it was the whole race, and by the second lap her legs felt like wet rope. Kale had beaten her three times this month, always the same way, pulling ahead while Natalie faded. Today she wanted to figure out why the fading happened, because it could not just be that Kale had more energy. She watched him jog the oval before the race, easy and relaxed, and she began to suspect the hidden cause. Maybe the problem was not her legs. Maybe it was her plan. The whole trouble might come from something she could not see, a mechanism inside the race itself: spend too much on lap one and lap two takes it back with interest.

She tested the idea with a small experiment. "Kale," she said, "today I'm going to run the first lap like I'm bored." He laughed. "Bored?" "Totally bored. Like I'm walking a dog." Conor, who was timing them, shook his head. "That's radical. You always go out fast." "That's the point," Natalie said. "If I'm right, going slow first is actually faster at the end."

The race started and the whole pack complied with nobody's plan except their own, which meant chaos. Two boys from Conor's class tore away like the finish line was fifty metres out. Natalie held back even though every part of her wanted to chase them, counting the cones as she passed, one, two, three, four, one lap. One of the sprinting boys crossed the line area and started pumping his arms, grinning, kicking for home. Conor yelled, "That's one lap! You've still got a whole lap!" The boy's face changed. He had lost count, and he had just spent his finish on nothing.

Kale and Natalie came around the last turn side by side. Natalie felt something she almost did not recognize: strength. She kicked, and for three strides she was ahead, and then Kale nudged past her by a shoulder. He won, but only by half a step, and his mouth was open like a fish. "You almost had me," he panted. "What happened to wet-rope legs?"

"I ran bored," Natalie said. She looked down at her legs, which were shaking but willing. "Tomorrow I'm going to run bored and then angry." Conor clicked his stopwatch and held it up. "Both laps faster than your old race. Both of them." Natalie grinned and started her cooldown lap, the cones counting themselves off behind her.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: A message sent in a private chat can be screenshotted and shared by anyone who receives it, so a private message is only as private as the people who read it.
story:
The lobby of Castle Rush filled fast on Saturday night, and Emile had one job: recruit a fifth player before the tournament sign-ups closed. His squad had four, and the clock gave them ten minutes. He scanned the names floating above the avatars until he spotted one he recognized, a player called FrostByte who had once carried a whole team with nothing but a rusty shield and a lot of shouting. "Perfect," Emile muttered, and typed into the public lobby chat, "FrostByte, we need you. We have snacks and a battle plan that almost works."

Christine, sitting two screens away in her own house but audible through voice chat, laughed. "Our battle plan is Emile running in first and the rest of us apologizing." In the lobby, other players chimed in with cheerful nonsense, all caps and exclamation points, the way public chat always sounded, loud and goofy and aimed at everyone at once. Emile switched to a private message, the quiet channel just between him and FrostByte, and wrote, "Ignore Christine, her aim is so bad the tutorial apologizes to her. Join us instead."

FrostByte joined. Then, a minute later, Christine's voice came through the headset, flat and dangerous. "Emile. Why is a screenshot of your private message in the team chat?" There it was on his screen, his own joke, cropped and pasted for the whole squad to see, including Christine. Only FrostByte had received it, and FrostByte had clearly passed it along. Emile felt his face go hot. "That was supposed to be just between us two," he typed, then realized how naive that sounded. A message sent to one person wasn't locked anywhere; it could be screenshotted and shared by anyone who got it, so it was only as private as the people who read it. He had assumed quiet meant safe, and the assumption had just bitten him.

He decided to test the rule before trusting anyone again. In a fresh private message to FrostByte he wrote, "Round two, FrostByte, this one's even worse," and then sent a second message only to Neveah, his other teammate: "Meet me at the west gate, I have a plan." If the first one surfaced in team chat and the second stayed quiet, he would know exactly who leaked. Two minutes later, FrostByte's screenshot appeared, this time with a caption, "he said round two lol." The west gate message went nowhere. Neveah, at least, could keep a secret.

Emile sent a genuine apology to Christine, public, in the lobby chat, where everyone could watch him eat his words. She made him duel her in the practice ring as payment, and she beat him three times in a row while Neveah commentated like a sports announcer. "The tutorial would like a rematch," Christine said, and offered him a hand up off the virtual dirt.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: If a knife starts to fall, step back and let it drop; trying to catch a falling knife is a common way to get cut.
story:
Nicholas had never been inside a restaurant kitchen before Saturday, when Ms. Rahman unlocked the back door of her little pasta place and let him, Edison, and Audrey in for a cooking lesson. He wanted to learn one thing properly: how to make a sauce from scratch, like his grandmother used to, because at home he only ever opened jars. Ms. Rahman gave each of them an onion and a knife and showed them the claw grip, fingers curled under so the knuckles, not the fingertips, faced the blade.

"Curl your fingers like you're holding a small stone," she said. "The knife rides against your knuckles."

Nicholas cut slowly, and his pieces came out uneven, but none of them came out bloody, which he counted as a win. Audrey's onion pieces were neat and fast. Edison kept dropping half-moons on the floor and blaming the cutting board. The kitchen smelled sharp and raw, and Ms. Rahman had already set a wide pan on the stove, ready for the sauce that would generate enough steam to fog the little window above the sink.

Then it happened. Edison bumped the counter with his hip, and his knife slid sideways, off the edge, handle first. Nicholas's arm shot out before he even thought about it, and Ms. Rahman's hand caught his sleeve and pulled him back a step. The knife hit the floor with a clatter and lay there, blade flat, wobbling once and going still.

"Let it fall," Ms. Rahman said. "A falling knife has no handle." She picked it up herself, wiped it, and set it back on the board. "Trying to catch a falling knife is a common way to get cut. Step back and let it drop."

Nicholas looked at his own hand. His instinct had been wrong, and he could see why now, without anyone spelling it out: the blade was where his fingers would have gone. He filed the rule away the same way he filed the claw grip, as something true about the world that you only find out by watching close. Edison swept the floor without being asked, as if the clatter had given him a sudden obligation.

The onions went into the pan and hissed. Nicholas stirred while Audrey crushed the tomatoes with her hands, and Edison added salt twice because nobody stopped him. The sauce bubbled and thickened and turned a deep, conventional red, the kind you see in every picture of pasta ever taken, except this one smelled like theirs. Ms. Rahman dipped a spoon, blew on it, and handed it to Nicholas.

He tasted. "It's better than the jar," he said, and reached for another spoon.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: U.S. sleep experts recommend 9 to 12 hours of sleep a night for children aged 6 to 12, and 8 to 10 hours for teenagers.
story:
Taylor's sneakers squeaked on the gym floor as she lined up with twenty other kids behind Coach Reyes, who would supervise the whole two-day tryout for the seventh-grade team. First drill: suicides. Taylor sprinted hard, lungs burning, and made her times. But halfway down the line she noticed Dalia stumbling through her turns, a step slow, like her feet were answering a beat everyone else could hear and she couldn't.

"You okay?" Taylor whispered while they waited for the next whistle.

"Fine," Dalia said, but her eyes wouldn't stay open all the way.

At water break, Taylor did some counting in her head. Dalia's little brother was on Taylor's bus, and he had told everyone this morning that Dalia was up until midnight beating some dragon boss. The bus came at 7:15. That was about seven hours of sleep, maybe less. Taylor remembered a chart in the nurse's office from last year's health unit: kids aged six to twelve need nine to twelve hours a night, and teenagers need eight to ten. Dalia was twelve, so seven wasn't even at the bottom of her range. Taylor felt a little jolt, the same one she got when a math problem suddenly made sense. Maybe Dalia wasn't lazy or out of shape. Maybe her legs were running on an empty battery.

But she could be wrong. Taylor decided to test it. If sleep was the hidden cause, then a kid with plenty of sleep should look fast, and a kid without it should look slow, and it should change when the sleep changed. She watched Kaylie, who was quick and sharp on every cut. "How'd you sleep?" Taylor asked her in the hallway.

"Like nine hours," Kaylie said. "My mom confiscates my phone at nine thirty."

That was one piece. Then Taylor needed the second half of her experiment, and that meant getting Dalia to actually sleep tonight, since tryouts continued tomorrow. At lunch she scribbled a note on a napkin and slid it across the table.

Dear Dalia,

I figured out why you looked like a zombie out there. You got about seven hours, and kids our age are supposed to get nine to twelve. Even teenagers only get to dip down to eight. Tonight: homework right after school, screens off, lights out by nine thirty. That's ten hours. Tomorrow we race and you prove me right. Deal?

Taylor

Dalia read it twice. "That's a little naive, don't you think?" she said. "You think one night of sleep fixes everything?"

"No," Taylor said. "I think it fixes today's problem. Tryouts are today and tomorrow. That's the only window we've got."

Dalia looked skeptical, and Taylor could see the skepticism in her folded arms, but she finally nodded. "Fine. But if I'm still slow, you owe me my dragon boss back."

The next afternoon, Taylor scanned the line before the whistle. Dalia was bouncing on her toes, actually bouncing, grinning at the ball like it owed her money. When Coach Reyes called the sprint ladder, Dalia beat her time from yesterday by a full second, then slapped Taylor five so hard it stung.

"Told you," Taylor said.

"You told me," Dalia said, already backing toward the shooting drill. "Now watch me make ten in a row."

She made eight, then nine, and the tenth ball hung on the rim, wobbled, and dropped clean through the net.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: Labeling each moving box with the room it belongs in and its contents makes unpacking faster, because boxes can be carried straight to the right place.
story:
Camille sat in the back seat with her knees against a box marked KITCHEN, MISC, and watched the last street of her old town slide past the window. Beside her, Dana's voice crackled through the phone propped on the armrest. "Promise you'll video call Thursday," Dana said. "Promise," Camille said. Then the houses thinned out, the road widened, and the call dropped.

The car was packed so full that Camille could not see over the towers of boxes. She leaned forward between the front seats. "Mom, which one has my bedsheets?" Her mom glanced at the side mirror. "No idea, honey. Somewhere in the back." Camille settled back and frowned at the wall of cardboard. Her dad had labeled some boxes with the room they belonged in and what was inside, because he was the organized one. Her mom had labeled others with a single word, MISC, because she was not.

Camille tried to remember the last move, three years ago, when she was eight. In the flashback she stood in the hallway of the old apartment while her parents opened box after box on the living room floor, hunting through them like archaeologists. Her bedsheets had turned up on the second night, buried under a lamp and a bag of extension cords. Every box back then had said MISC. Was that a coincidence? She despised coincidences that hid a pattern, and she wondered if there was one here. Maybe unlabeled boxes were slow for a reason she could test.

She ran a quiet experiment in her head. The labeled boxes could be carried straight to the room they belonged in and unpacked without digging. The MISC boxes had to be opened somewhere, searched, and their contents carried around the house piece by piece, like the boxes three years ago. It seemed almost a paradox, that a few seconds with a marker could save hours of searching, but the logic held. Still, she knew she could be biased toward her dad's tidy way of doing things, so she wanted proof. She counted on her fingers: nineteen labeled boxes, seven MISC. Enough for a fair comparison.

"Can we keep a tally?" she asked. "When we unpack tonight, we time the labeled boxes against the MISC ones." Her dad grinned at her in the mirror. "You're on."

The new house rose up at the end of a gravel lane, porch light already on. A neighbor across the street, Ms. Morales, waved from her garden as the car doors opened one by one. Camille climbed out, pulled the phone from her pocket, and snapped a picture of the box wall. Then she picked up the nearest labeled box, KITCHEN, POTS, and carried it straight through the front door and into the kitchen, setting it on the counter beside the stove. "One," she called over her shoulder. "Start the clock."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The word diaspora comes from a Greek word meaning scattering, and it describes a people living spread out far from the homeland of their ancestors.
story:
Lionel's kitchen smelled like scorched coconut, and his grandmother was fanning the smoke away with a folded newspaper. On the table behind her lay a half-painted banner for Saturday's cultural festival, and Anthony could read it upside down: THE JAMAICAN DIASPORA OF MAPLEWOOD, in green letters with one D still unpainted.

"Lionel, what's diaspora?" Anthony asked.

Lionel shrugged. "Grandma said to put it on the banner. I think it's like a group of people." Crystal, who was lettering a smaller sign at the counter, tilted her head. "Nobody at the community centre table could tell me either. The man just said it sounded important."

Anthony pulled out his phone. "If we're going to stand under this thing all Saturday, we should know what it says." He typed the word in, then read the screen twice to be sure he had it right. "It comes from a Greek word meaning scattering," he said slowly. "And it describes a people living spread out far from the homeland of their ancestors."

There was a silence except for the grandmother's newspaper flapping. Then she set it down and looked at the banner, and at Anthony, and something in her face went soft.

"My mother came from Saint Elizabeth parish," she said. "Her sisters went to London and Toronto. Their children went farther still. Scattered like seeds, all of us, and still Jamaican." She tapped the banner. "That is the word for us."

Crystal got out her marker and started making small cards with the definition copied out, one for each person at the table, so that if visitors asked, anybody could answer. Lionel painted the last D with careful strokes, because a banner about a word nobody understood seemed worse than no banner at all. Anthony tested his idea out loud: if diaspora meant scattering, then the festival itself was what happened after the scattering, all those seeds landing in one gymnasium in Maplewood and growing food and music and banners together. The others considered this and returned a unanimous verdict: exceptional theory, worth putting on a card too.

The grandmother laughed and brought out a plate of patties, including the one burnt edge she'd cut off, which she slid toward Anthony because he'd arrived first and looked hungry. Outside, a breeze came through the screen door and lifted the corner of the wet banner, and Lionel lunged across the table to hold it down with both palms.

"Not yet," he told it. "You scatter on Saturday."

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: In a fair test, every other condition is kept the same, so any difference in results can be traced to the one variable that was changed.
story:
Evan spread his science notebook across the library table and frowned at the photos taped inside. Six weeks of bean plants, and his results made no sense. The pot he had watered with the plant food had grown three centimeters less than the plain-water pot. That was backwards.

"You look like your project bit you," Eddie said, dropping into the chair across from him.

"It did. Look." Evan turned the notebook so Eddie could see the chart. "I wanted to quantify the growth difference, so I measured both plants every Friday. The food plant should have won."

Eddie leaned in. "Where did you keep them?"

"Kitchen counter." Evan stopped. He flipped back to the first photo, taken the day he planted the seeds. In the background of the picture, one pot sat on the windowsill above the sink, and the other sat on the counter by the fridge. He had moved them around when his mother needed the sill for herbs, and he had never written down which pot was where on which day.

He remembered his teacher, Mr. Warsame, holding up two identical cups of water at the start of the year. Aleksandra had been the one who named it. "A fair test," she had said. "You change one thing and keep everything else the same." Evan had nodded then, but he had never really thought about how easy it was to break that rule without noticing.

"The window," he said slowly. "One plant got sunlight half the day and the other one didn't. I changed two things, not one. So I can't tell if the food helped or hurt." He tapped the photo. "Any difference in my results could be from the light, or the food, or both."

"So your whole experiment is trash?"

"No." Evan was already pulling a blank data sheet from his backpack. "It's one amendment to my plan, that's all. I'm going to redo it. Same seeds, same soil, same amount of water, same spot side by side under the same lamp. The only thing I change is the food. Then whatever difference shows up has to come from that one thing."

Eddie grinned. "You're weirdly happy about your project falling apart."

"Because now it's authentic," Evan said. "Before, I just had numbers. Now I actually know what they mean." He stood, gathered the notebook, and headed for the front desk to ask how many bean seeds he could check out from the seed library.

activity: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
knowledge_domain: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
fact: The Treaty of Versailles limited the German army to 100,000 soldiers and banned Germany from having an air force.
story:
Gavin sat on his grandfather's porch steps with his history notebook open on his knees, staring at the question Ms. Francis had written on the board before vacation: How did the Treaty of Versailles help lead to the Second World War? He was supposed to explain it in a paragraph when school started again, and so far his page held only the word "Because."

"You look like a boy trying to diagnose a car that won't start," his grandfather said, coming out with two glasses of lemonade.

"I have to explain a treaty," Gavin said. "It limited Germany's army after World War One. That's all I know. But then World War Two happened, so did the limit not matter? Was it a bad treaty? I can't figure out what to write."

His grandfather settled into the wicker chair. "Walk with me after your lemonade. There's a memorial at the corner of the cemetery, names from both wars on the same stone."

They walked down the gravel lane, past the fence and the rows of markers. The memorial was a gray obelisk, shorter than Gavin expected. On one face the names from the first war crowded together, and on the facing side, the second war's names started lower down. Gavin ran his finger along them.

"The army was limited to one hundred thousand soldiers," he said slowly. "That's fewer people than a lot of cities. And Germany wasn't allowed an air force at all. So a country that big, told it could barely have soldiers and no planes. That's like taking away someone's lunch every single day."

"Somebody took your lunch once," his grandfather said.

"Andrei did, in fourth grade, before he was my friend. For a week I just took it. Then I got so angry I shoved him into the fence, and we both got in trouble." Gavin looked at the stone again. "The treaty did the first part. It told Germany it was small when it wasn't. Then somebody promised to make Germany big and strong again, and people listened because the anger was already there."

He pulled the notebook out of his back pocket and wrote while standing, hunched over the obelisk's base. Later, back at the house, he read his paragraph aloud over dinner. His grandmother stopped peeling potatoes to listen. His grandfather said it was the most robust argument anyone had made at that table since his uncle debated the whole family about heritage tomatoes versus regular ones.

On the first morning back, Ms. Francis asked for volunteers. Andrei's hand shot up, and behind him Abdullah elbowed Gavin until he raised his too. When Gavin finished reading, his voice steadier than he expected, Ms. Francis said, "You explained cause and effect better than the textbook does."

At recess, Andrei found him by the fence. "You compared a whole country to me stealing a sandwich."

"To you stealing my sandwich," Gavin said, and Andrei laughed so hard he had to sit down on the curb.

activity: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
knowledge_domain: to compare a stock and a bond and explain which is riskier and why
fact: If a company fails completely, its stock price can fall to zero, so a stockholder can lose every dollar they put in.
story:
Peyton slapped three quarters onto the picnic table beside her lemonade stand and counted the morning's earnings out loud. "Fourteen dollars and fifty cents. Mr. Pelletier, if you buy two more cups, I can hit twenty by noon." Her neighbor chuckled and held out his glass for a refill.

Mustafa pedaled up the driveway on his bike, dropped it in the grass, and grabbed a cup without asking. "Did you hear about Josh?" he said. Peyton leaned forward, napkins still in her hand. "He put all his birthday money into that company everybody was shouting about, the one from the videos. Sixty dollars, every dollar he had." Mustafa drained half the cup. "My brother says the whole thing fell apart. Josh's sixty dollars turned into zero. Nothing left."

Peyton set down the pitcher. Her mouth went dry even with lemonade in it. Last week in Mr. Pelletier's garage, while he fixed her bike chain, he had asked her whether she would rather own a piece of a company or lend money to one. She had shrugged then. Now her brain was racing. Owning a piece, a stock, meant if the company grew, your piece grew. But if the company failed completely, the stock price could fall all the way to zero, and you could lose every dollar you put in. Josh had just lived that.

"Lending is different," she said slowly, watching condensation drip off the pitcher. "If you lend a company money, a bond, you're not owning anything. You just expect to be paid back." She flipped over a paper cup and drew two columns with a marker, stock on one side, bond on the other. "Josh owns a piece of nothing now. Zero." Her conscience pricked her a little, sketching out his disaster on a lemonade cup, but she wanted to understand it before she felt sorry about it.

"That's why stocks are riskier," Mustafa said, peering at the cup. Peyton nodded so fast her ponytail bounced. "Risk isn't just prices wiggling around. It's the whole thing going to zero."

A car pulled up and Josh himself climbed out, holding an empty jar. He walked over slowly. "My mom said I should earn some money back. Got a job for me?"

Peyton looked at her pitcher, half full, then at the twenty-dollar goal written on her sign. She handed him the marker. "Write your name under mine. But first, one rule." She tapped the paper cup with the two columns. "Nobody puts the whole cashbox into one thing. We restrict ourselves to spending on cups and sugar, and we split what's left. Deal?"

Josh uncapped the marker and grinned for the first time all morning. "Deal. Now hand me a lemon."

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: A metal wire's resistance rises as it heats up, so Ohm's law gives a steady resistance only while the wire's temperature stays the same.
story:
Taylor crouched beside the fold-up table at the edge of the skate park, holding a multimeter in both hands like it might bolt. Her science project was due Friday, and she had one shot tonight. The idea was simple: measure the voltage across a wire, measure the current through it, divide, and get the wire's resistance. Oceanne had promised to write down every number, and Brayden had promised to keep the skaters from grinding over the equipment.

"Three point four volts," Taylor read off the screen. "Current is one point seven amps. Write it down." Oceanne scratched the number into her notebook while a board rattled past on the concrete behind them. Taylor did the division twice in her head. "Two ohms. Okay, that's our answer. Two ohms."

"Want to check it again?" Oceanne asked. She was the kind of friend who double-checked everything, including her own locker combination.

Taylor ran the test again. Same wire, same battery pack, same clips biting the same spots. "Three point six volts. One point seven amps." She frowned. That came out to a bit more than two ohms. Not much more, but more. She waited a minute, letting a plane drone overhead and the smell of hot rubber drift from the halfpipe, then ran it a third time. The number crept up again.

"That's weird," Brayden said, rolling back toward them with his helmet crooked. "The wire doesn't change. Same wire, same everything. How can the answer change?"

Taylor touched the wire with one fingertip and pulled back fast. It was warm, warmer than the evening air, warmer than it had been when they started. She looked at her three scribbled results. The first reading had come right after they clipped everything together, back when the wire was still cool. The last one came after the current had been flowing for a while. "It's hot," she said slowly. "The wire's hot, and the answer got bigger. Every time."

Oceanne flipped back a page in her notebook. "So when it was cool, we got two. Then a little more. Then a little more again." She tapped her pencil on the numbers like she was playing them on a piano.

Taylor unclipped the battery and let the wire sit. She watched Oceanne sketch a ramp in the margin and Brayden attempt, badly, to distribute the leftover granola bars into three uneven piles. After ten minutes she touched the wire again. Cool. She clipped the battery back on, took one fast reading, and then made herself wait, counting under her breath while the wire warmed, taking readings at each minute mark. The resistance climbed, small step after small step, the whole way up.

"It only holds still when the temperature holds still," Taylor said, copying the numbers into a clean column. "So the steady answer, the real one for a cool wire, is that first quick reading. The rest is the wire heating up under the test." She looked at Oceanne's notebook, then at her own, and felt something settle that felt almost like landing a trick. "We'll take the reading fast, before it warms. And we'll say so right on the poster."

"Mr. Yang is going to think we made that up," Oceanne said, but she was already underlining the column, pressing hard enough that the pencil made a robust, dark line.

"He'll test it himself," Taylor said. "That's the good part." She picked up the multimeter and clipped the leads back on for one more run, just to watch the first number come out clean.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: In both 1995 and 1996 David Justice had a higher batting average than Derek Jeter, yet Jeter's average for the two years combined was higher.
story:
The library computers were supposed to be for the history project, but Justin had baseball-reference open in one tab and a page about medieval peasants in the other, and the baseball tab was winning. He was supposed to be writing about farming in the Middle Ages, and he had gotten exactly one sentence down, something about how a peasant worked the same strips of field year after year. His friend Mickael leaned over from the next computer.

"Look up David Justice versus Derek Jeter," Mickael said. "Me and my uncle argued about it all weekend. Justice was better in the nineties, no question."

Justin typed the names in. The comparison page loaded, and he scrolled to the batting averages. In 1995, Justice was higher than Jeter. In 1996, Justice was higher again. "See?" Mickael said. "Twice in a row. Case closed."

But there was a third row, the combined line for both seasons together, and Justin stopped with his finger halfway to the screen. Combined, Jeter was higher. He read it twice, then clicked the little button that split the page year by year, thinking maybe the site had made a mistake. It hadn't. Justice won 1995. Justice won 1996. Add them together and Jeter won.

"Lexa," Justin called across the library, not quite loud enough to get them kicked out. "Come look at this. It's broken."

Lexa had her own project on her screen, a poster about flood statistics for the science fair, and she was hunting for a number impressive enough to print in big letters. She dragged her chair over anyway, because Lexa could never resist a puzzle. Justin showed her the three lines. "He beats him both years and loses both years added up. How is that even possible?"

"That's like my flood numbers," Lexa said slowly, tapping the screen. "One big flood year can swing everything, and the headline just squishes it into one number." She narrowed her eyes. "Who decides which number becomes the headline, though? That's what I want to know."

Mr. Bighorn, the librarian, paused behind them on his rounds, but he only looked at the screen, raised one eyebrow, and moved on toward the shelf returns without a word.

Justin sat back. All afternoon, the sports page and the news had been handing him single numbers, and he had just accepted them, the way he'd accepted that the Middles Ages were one gray lump of mud. He wondered how many of those numbers were hiding something the way this one was. Maybe the trick was being systematic, checking the pieces every single time instead of trusting the summary. He couldn't prove that yet, but it felt like the kind of thing a person could quantify, counting how often a headline number matched its own parts.

"Forget my uncle," Mickael said, pulling out his phone. "He's going to lose his mind when I show him this. Text me the link."

"First," Justin said, "help me pick a headline number for Lexa's poster."

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: Freytag's pyramid, based on Gustav Freytag's 1863 book on drama, pictures a plot as rising to the climax at its peak and then falling.
story:
Colton stared at his story draft and counted the quotation marks. Seven. Four of them opened dialogue and three closed it, which meant somewhere a character was still talking, possibly forever. Ms. Teo had circled the mess in red and written "Clarify who is speaking!" at the top. The story was about a giant mutant larva that crawled out of the compost bin behind the cafeteria, and it was supposed to be his best work of the year, but right now it read like a ransom note.

"Your larva story?" Reese said at lunch, leaning over his shoulder. She pulled out her own draft and flipped it to the back, where she had sketched a mountain. "Look. I draw my whole plot like this. Rising action climbs the slope, the climax sits at the peak, and everything after falls back down the other side." She tapped the summit. "My peak is when the mask comes off. It's called Freytag's pyramid. Some German guy, Gustav Freytag, wrote a book about drama in 1863, and that's where it comes from."

"That's radical," Colton said. "But where's my peak? My larva just eats stuff for two pages and then it's Tuesday."

"Exactly. You've got a hill, not a mountain. Put something huge at the top and then let it fall." She slid the paper toward him. "Also, new speaker, new paragraph. That fixes half your punctuation."

Colton spent the evening testing her idea on graph paper. He drew the pyramid, wrote LARVA EATS THE PRINCIPAL'S CAR at the peak, and then mapped the falling side: the larva shrinks, the town forgives it, the science club adopts it as a mascot. When his mom asked why he was drawing triangles on his homework, he said, "Plot geometry," and she left him alone. The dialogue he rewrote line by line, whispering each part in a different voice so he could hear where one speaker stopped and the next one started. Whenever a line needed a tag, he added one; whenever two lines in a row belonged to the same mouth, he joined them.

The next morning he handed his draft to Shane, who read it silently and then aloud, doing the larva as a monster truck announcer. Every quotation mark landed where it should. "The car scene gave me chills," Shane said. "Actual chills."

At the end of class, Ms. Teo held up Colton's paper. "This one works," she said. "Strong peak, clean fall, and I can always tell who's talking." Colton grinned at Reese across the room and drew a tiny triangle in the corner of his notebook, then wrote one word inside it: sequel.

activity: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
knowledge_domain: to run a club meeting with an agenda so everyone gets a chance to speak
fact: "Agenda" is a Latin word meaning "things to be done," and a meeting agenda lists the topics in the order they will be discussed.
story:
Victor tapped the whiteboard marker against his palm and stared at the blank whiteboard like it had insulted him. In twenty minutes, the Geography Club would file into Room 12, and he would run his first real meeting as president. Last month's meeting had been a disaster he still could not diagnose: forty minutes on whether to buy cheese crackers or pretzels for the fundraiser, and then the bell rang before anyone discussed the actual fundraiser. He had replayed it in his head all week and finally landed on a hidden cause. Nobody had written down what else to discuss, so the snack question, being the only question on the table, had swallowed everything.

Paisley arrived first, dropped her backpack on a desk, and eyed the empty whiteboard with open skepticism. "You have a plan this time, or are we voting on crackers again?"

"We are not," Victor said, and he wrote AGENDA in tall letters.

Anouk slid in behind her. "Ooh, official." She pronounced it "ah-GEN-dah," like a spell.

"It's Latin," Victor said. "It means things to be done." He had found that out Tuesday, in the dictionary, while pretending to research rivers. "And it lists the topics in the order we'll discuss them." He wrote 1. Fundraiser, 2. Field trip, 3. Snacks, and put a hard little period after the 3.

"Snacks last?" Paisley said. "Bold."

"Snacks last," Victor said, "because snacks can survive until 3:40. The field trip cannot."

Mr. Tse poked his head in, since the club was technically his to supervise. He studied the board, raised one eyebrow, and said only, "Carry on," which felt like a medal.

The meeting began, and Victor discovered that an agenda was a leash made of paper. When Paisley started a lush, wandering story about her cousin's trip to a rainforest exhibit, Victor tapped item one. "Table that under field trip inspiration," he said, and Paisley grinned and steered back to poster paper prices. When Anouk debated whether the raffle prize should be a globe or an atlas, he pointed to item two, and the field trip conversation absorbed the question like a sponge. Twenty minutes in, they had chosen a poster format, picked the museum, and even settled the globe-atlas fight, because the museum gift shop sold both.

"Item three," Victor announced, feeling like a game show host.

"Cheese crackers," Paisley and Anouk said together, then looked delighted with themselves.

"Pretzels," said Victor, and everyone groaned, and the bell rang before the argument could eat anything but the last four minutes.

Anouk pulled on her backpack and paused at the door. "Same agenda thing next time?"

"Same agenda thing," Victor said, and underlined the 3 on the board one extra time, just for the crackers.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: American sociologist Ruth Hill Useem coined the term 'third culture kid' in the 1950s for children raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture.
story:
"Where are you from?" asked Ms. Kelly, and the new girl, Isa, opened her mouth and then closed it again.

The class discussion was supposed to be about heritage posters. Everyone had brought one: Kaley had taped up photos of her grandmother's village, and Anais had drawn a map of her mother's hometown with arrows pointing to everywhere the family had lived since. But Isa had come in with nothing, and now she stood at the front of Ms. Kelly's room twisting the strap of her backpack.

"I've lived in four countries," Isa said. "My dad works for a company that moves us. But when people ask where I'm from, I don't know what to say. My parents' home culture isn't mine, really. I wasn't born in most of the places we lived. So." She shrugged and stared at the floor tiles.

Anais's hand went up before she had decided to raise it. Last year a boy had asked her the same question in the cafeteria, and she had said the name of her mother's town, even though she had never lived there, and the answer had felt like a coat that belonged to somebody else. She had thought about that lie for months. "There's a word for it," she said now. "I found it when I was making my poster. My aunt has it too. A sociologist named Ruth Hill Useem, in the 1950s, coined the term 'third culture kid' for children raised in a culture different from their parents' home culture."

Isa looked up. "Third culture kid. Say it again?"

"Third culture kid," Anais said, and the words sat differently in the room than the map on the wall behind her.

Kaley frowned. "So you're from a country that doesn't exist?"

"Sort of from all of them and none of them," Isa said slowly, like she was testing a bridge with her foot before stepping on it. She pulled a marker from her backpack and went to the whiteboard. "Can I make my poster out of this? Four flags, and then a box in the middle that just says TCK?"

"That's the assignment, more or less," Ms. Kelly said, and moved aside.

Isa drew fast, four rectangles and a crooked box, and under it wrote her name, her real one, the one that had never needed a country attached. She tapped the box twice with the marker and turned around. "Okay," she said. "Next question."

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: A damp cloth or damp paper towel under a cutting board stops the board from sliding across the counter while you chop.
story:
At the Saturday farmers' market, Xavier stood in front of Ms. Lau's stall, where the tomatoes were piled so lush and red they looked like they had been painted that morning. He was on a mission. His grandmother had declared that anyone who wanted dinner at her table on Sunday had to help make it, and he had volunteered for the sauce. That meant onions, and onions meant chopping, which he had never done.

"Take a bag of the Romas," Ms. Lau said, weighing three onions, "and hold the knife like this when you cut." She curved her fingers inward on an invisible onion, knuckles forward, thumb tucked behind. "Claw grip. Your knuckles guide the blade, so it can't reach your fingertips." Xavier practiced the shape with his hand. It felt like a small, stubborn animal.

Back home, he set up on the counter and started to chop. The moment he pressed down, the cutting board shot sideways and the knife skidded off the onion. He tried again, slower. The board slid again, and the blade landed crooked, nowhere near where he'd aimed. He stared at the board. The counter was smooth, the board was smooth, and every push of the knife nudged the whole thing away like a hockey puck. That was the problem, he realized. Not his grip. The board itself.

He thought about what slid and what didn't. A wet bath mat didn't slide. The market's signs didn't blow away when the vendor weighted them with damp cloths on windy days. Maybe wet was the key. He ran a paper towel under the tap, wrung it out, and laid it flat under the cutting board. Then he curled his hand into the claw grip, set the blade against the onion, and pushed down. The board held. He chopped a full slice, then another, and the board stayed planted as if it had been glued. His eyes stung and watered, but he kept going, dicing the whole onion into small, even pieces.

On Sunday, his grandmother tasted the sauce, which had simmered with the market tomatoes, garlic, and a pinch of sugar, and asked where he'd learned to chop like a real cook. Xavier drafted his little cousin over to the counter to demonstrate. He ran a towel under the tap, placed it under the board, curved his fingers into the claw, and handed the boy a butter knife and half a banana.

"Every good consumer of onions should know this trick," he said, and his cousin laughed and chopped a slice clean through.

activity: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
knowledge_domain: to build a spreadsheet with a formula that adds a column and makes a bar chart
fact: A spreadsheet cell's address is its column letter followed by its row number, so C4 is the cell in column C, row 4.
story:
The spreadsheet was supposed to be easy, but Isla's numbers kept arguing with her. She was entering data for the science fair, burn times for four kinds of fabric, because her project asked which cloth was most flammable and how long each one took to catch. Ms. Rosen had shown the class once, back in September, and now the whole thing hinged on Isla remembering something she had half forgotten. The bell had rung, the lab was nearly empty, and her chart showed a bar taller than the ceiling for cotton and nothing at all for wool.

Then Veronica called from the kitchen, where the two of them had done the actual burning with Isla's dad and a pair of long tongs. "Okay, I found the paper," Veronica said. "Wool, forty seconds, and it's in 4C."

"4C," Isla repeated, and typed 40 into cell 4C, except there was no cell 4C, because the rows were numbered and the columns were lettered, going across. The screen put her 40 somewhere on the wrong side of everything. She stared at it. The columns ran A, B, C, left to right, and the rows ran 1, 2, 3, going down. So an address had to start with the letter. She said it out loud to herself. "C4 is the cell in column C, row 4." She dragged the 40 down to C4, where it belonged.

"Did you say something?" Veronica asked.

"I said your directions are backwards. It's C4, not 4C."

"I was reading it off the paper sideways," Veronica said, which explained nothing and made them both laugh so hard the phone crackled.

Isla checked the rest of the column. Two more numbers had landed in the wrong row because she had rushed, which was why her sum had seemed impossible, and why the bar for cotton had towered over everything like it was trying to oppose the ceiling itself. She fixed each one, then clicked the empty cell at the bottom of the column and typed =SUM(C1:C4). The total appeared, small and believable, like a dog that had finally stopped barking.

The bar chart rebuilt itself as she watched, four bars of sensible heights, denim tallest, wool shortest. Edison leaned over from the next computer, where he was supposed to be logging out. "That's actually a decent chart," he said, which from Edison was practically a standing ovation.

"Tell that to the wool," Isla said, and hit print.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japanese homes, shoes are taken off in an entrance area called the genkan before stepping inside.
story:
The invitation said Sakura House, and Theodore assumed it was just a restaurant until he pushed through the front door and nearly stepped on a row of shoes. Sneakers, loafers, one small pair of rain boots, all lined up on a lower floor of polished wood that dipped a step below the main level. Beyond it, the whole space opened up: tatami mats, low tables, and a counter where Lou's grandmother was arranging chopsticks like piano keys. Theodore stood at the edge, one sneaker hovering over the wood.

"You're in the genkan," Lou said, appearing from behind a curtain with a stack of menus. "The entrance. Shoes come off here, before you go inside."

Theodore stepped back onto the lower floor and unlaced his sneakers. A pair of slippers sat waiting in a neat spot, and he was almost certain they had not been there a second ago, which meant someone had noticed him coming and set them out on purpose. He slid his feet in. The slippers were slightly too big, but they made a soft shuffling sound that he decided he liked.

Lou's family owned the restaurant, and tonight they were having a celebration dinner for Lou's birthday, which was the whole reason Theodore was there. The problem was the gift. He had wrapped his present, a book about chess, in newspaper because his mother had used all the wrapping paper on her cousin's wedding gift, and now, watching Lou's grandmother present Lou with a small box wrapped in cloth so intricate it looked like origami, Theodore felt the newspaper in his bag like a stone.

At the low table, Theodore discovered more rules. Lou's father clapped his hands together before eating, quick and light, and everyone murmured something together, so Theodore clapped too, half a beat late. When Lou's grandmother poured tea into Theodore's cup, he picked it up and drank, and then noticed that nobody else had touched theirs yet. Lou leaned over. "We wait until everyone's poured. It's how we do it here. At Ivana's house you just start, remember? Her dad gets insulted if you don't eat everything fast."

Theodore filed that away. At his own house the rules were different again: elbows off the table, fork in the left hand because his grandfather said so, and no reaching past anyone's plate. He began to wonder whether there was some hidden pattern underneath all of it, some rule behind the rules. Maybe every family had a list nobody wrote down, and the only way to learn it was to watch for the moment when everyone did the same thing at the same time. He decided to test the idea right there. When the rice arrived, he kept his hands in his lap and his eyes on Lou's father, waiting.

The moment came with the gift. Lou's grandmother handed over the cloth-wrapped box, and Lou received it with both hands, bowed his head slightly, and then set it beside him, unopened. Theodore, who at his own birthday parties had torn paper off in front of everyone within ten seconds, watched carefully. So that was the rule here: gifts got both hands, and they waited. He reached into his bag, and before he could evaluate whether newspaper was too embarrassing, he held the lumpy package out with both hands, the way Lou had received the box.

Lou took it the same way, and his grandmother said something to his father that made them both smile. "She says you learn fast," Lou translated, tucking the present beside him, unopened.

Theodore bowed his head, just a little, and reached for his teacup.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In one-point perspective, objects of the same real size, like lampposts along a street, are drawn smaller and closer together the farther away they are.
story:
Wyatt sat at the wobbly picnic table behind the art cabin, staring at his drawing of Main Street. He had drawn the road, the shops, and six lampposts, and every lamppost was exactly the same height, evenly spaced like fence posts. Lena leaned over his shoulder.

"It looks like a wall with lampposts glued on it," she said. "Not a street."

Wyatt was skeptical. "They're the same size in real life. Lampposts don't shrink."

Rayden slid his own drawing across the table. His street looked like it went somewhere. His lampposts started tall at the bottom of the page and got smaller and squeezed closer together until they nearly touched a single point far up the road. "Mr. Hu calls it the vanishing point," Rayden said. "All the lines go there."

Wyatt looked back and forth between the two drawings. His eye kept sliding along Rayden's street like it was being transported down the road itself. He took a fresh sheet and drew a horizon line, then one dot in the middle of it. He ran two lines from the bottom corners of the page straight to the dot, like railway tracks, and the space between them became the road.

Then the lampposts. He drew the first one big, right at the bottom edge. The second one he made smaller and put it a little farther along. The third smaller still, and closer to the next one. By the fifth, the lampposts were little more than pencil ticks, bunched together near the dot. It felt wrong, like lying about how tall lampposts were, but he kept going.
