He held the drawing up next to Rayden's. Lena walked over and looked at both. "Yours goes back farther," she said. "Mine still looks flat." She took Rayden's pencil and started her own vanishing point.

Mr. Hu came around the cabin with his clipboard. He picked up Wyatt's first attempt, the flat wall one, and studied it. "You drew every post the same height," he said. "Same distance apart, too." Then he picked up the second drawing and didn't say anything at all for a moment.

"That one's mine," said a voice from behind the cabins. A kid Wyatt had never seen before, maybe thirteen, with paint on his sleeves, reached over and took the second drawing out of Mr. Hu's hand. "I left it on the table this morning."

Wyatt stared at the sheet in the kid's hand. He was certain he had drawn it, five minutes ago, on fresh paper. Then he looked down at the table, at the smudge of graphite by the clipboard, and at his own pencil, which had been sharpened that morning and was now suddenly long again.

"Where's my drawing?" Wyatt asked.

The kid flipped the sheet over. On the back, in Wyatt's own handwriting, it said, WYATT, TABLE 4. "Transport yourself to table four," the kid said, "and look under it." Wyatt crouched down. Taped beneath the table was his real drawing, the one with the shrinking lampposts, folded into a paper airplane pointed straight at the vanishing point of the room's far corner.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Clothes left crumpled in a dryer or basket after the cycle ends tend to wrinkle as they cool, so taking them out promptly and folding them helps keep them smooth.
story:
On Saturday morning, Gabriel stood beside his brother in the lobby of First Regional Bank, holding a garment bag. His brother had a job interview with the branch manager in twenty minutes, and his one good shirt was a disaster.

"It looks like it slept in a ball," his brother said, pulling it out. Creases ran across the front in hard lines, deep ones that no amount of stretching would fix.

Gabriel knew exactly how it had slept in a ball. The night before, he had run his first solo load of laundry while his brother was at work. He had sorted the colours carefully, following the phone call with Flynn, who had opinions about everything. "Separate the darks," Flynn had said, "and hot water shrinking things is controversial, so just use warm." Gabriel had stuffed the shirt into the dryer, heard the buzzer, and then gone to watch a video. He figured he would fold everything in the morning. What was the rush?

That morning, the shirt had come out of the dryer looking like a crumpled paper bag. Gabriel had pulled it out, laid it flat, and tried to smooth it with his hands. The wrinkles stayed. His brother had already left for the bank in his undershirt with a jacket over it, planning to change in the restroom, and he had texted Gabriel to bring the shirt.

Gabriel had an idea. He filled a spray bottle with water, dampened the shirt all over, and ran it back through the dryer for ten minutes while he stood there and watched it tumble the whole time. When the buzzer went off, he took it out immediately and folded it, warm, flat, and smooth. He slid it into the garment bag and rode his bike downtown.

In the bank restroom, his brother changed and looked in the mirror. The collar sat flat. The front was clean. "What did you do?"

"Ran it again and grabbed it the second it stopped," Gabriel said. "I left it in there all night before. That was the problem. You have to take stuff out right away and fold it, or it cools all crumpled."

His brother checked his tie in the mirror, then his watch. Waiting longer would only prolong his nerves, so he opened the restroom door and walked out into the lobby. A woman in a grey blazer was waiting by the desks with a folder in her hand.

"That's her," his brother whispered. "Wish me luck."

Gabriel gave him a thumbs up from the bench by the waiting area and texted Flynn: load one complete. Nobody lost a sock, the towels are folded, and I am never leaving anything in the dryer again.

Behind him, the teller called, "Next in line?" Gabriel stood, gathered the garment bag, and dropped the empty hanger into the trash.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: The periodic table arranges the elements in order of increasing atomic number, so each element has one more proton than the element before it.
story:
Georgia spread her homework across the kitchen table and stared at the periodic table Ms. Ma had photocopied for the whole class. Tomorrow's quiz asked for the number of protons in an element, and Georgia had exactly one clue: the tiny number above each square. She was pretty sure it mattered, but she could not remember how.

Frederick arrived first, dropping his backpack on the counter and stealing a handful of crackers from the box above the toaster. Chad came next, still holding his lacrosse stick, because Chad brought the lacrosse stick everywhere, even to study sessions he had not been invited to. "You're only here," Georgia said, "because your mom said no screens until your science grade improves." Chad shrugged. "That is a legitimate reason. Also there are crackers."

They bent over the photocopy together. "Okay," Frederick said, tapping the top row. "Hydrogen, then helium. There's a one, then a two." His finger slid down the poster. "Lithium, three. Beryllium, four. It's counting." Georgia felt something click, the way a puzzle piece does when you stop forcing it. "It counts up by one, all the way across." She flipped to the back of her worksheet, where Ms. Ma had written atomic number in the instructions, and looked again at the little numbers. "So the atomic number for oxygen is eight," she said slowly, "and the quiz wants protons."

She tested it the only way she could. She covered the poster with her hand and asked Frederick to name an element. "Carbon," he said. Georgia moved her hand just enough to peek. "Six. Carbon has six protons." She tried three more, and each time the pattern held, the numbers marching along in order, one more than the square before it. She wrote them down, checking twice.

Chad, meanwhile, had his own plan. "If I memorize the first ten elements tonight, Ms. Ma will let me back on the field by Thursday," he said, pacing the kitchen and chanting, "Hydrogen, helium, lithium." He paused at the window where the neighbor's cat sat watching them. "She's judging me." "That cat is not your colleague," Frederick said. "She has no idea what you're achieving tonight."

When Georgia's dad came in to start dinner, the table was covered with numbered scraps of paper and Chad had made it to neon without stopping. Georgia read her list once more, then again with her eyes shut. Eight protons in oxygen, six in carbon, one in hydrogen, each element exactly one more than the one before it all the way down the table. She slid the paper into her folder and zipped it shut. "Quiz me at breakfast," she said, and Chad, triumphant, said, "Neon. Ten."

activity: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
knowledge_domain: to explain how a monsoon forms and why it matters for rice farming in South Asia
fact: The India Meteorological Department gives June 1 as the normal date for the southwest monsoon to reach Kerala, on India's southwestern coast.
story:
Landon stood at the departure gate with his phone in one hand and his notes in the other, trying to explain monsoons to Kiera before their flight to visit his grandmother in Kerala. She was supposed to present with him in Ms. Rajapakse's class next week, and the whole thing depended on him getting it right.

"So the land heats up in summer," Kiera said, squinting at his messy diagram, "and then it rains for months? That part I get. But why does rice farming care?"

Landon glanced at the big window, where heat shimmered off the runway. He tried an experiment. He held his palm above his phone, which had been running warm in the sun, and then above the metal armrest of the chair. The phone felt like a stove; the armrest, which sat in the shade under his bag, stayed cool. "The land is like my phone," he said slowly. "It heats differently than the ocean. That difference is the hidden cause, I think. You can't see it, but it drags the wind, and the wind drags the rain."

"Okay," Kiera said. "But when does it actually arrive? A farmer can't plant rice on a hypothetical date. Rice needs water at the right time or the whole season fails."

Landon wanted to give up. He had rewritten his notes three times already on the flight from school to this connecting airport, and his hand was cramped. "Ask me something I know," he muttered. Kiera persevered anyway, flipping through his notes until she found a photo of a wall calendar from his grandmother's house. Every June, his grandmother circled the first of the month in red pen. When he was small, he had thought it was her birthday.

"That's it," Kiera said, tapping the photo. "That's the date."

Landon remembered his grandmother pointing at the calendar two summers ago, saying, "June 1. The India Meteorological Department calls that the normal date for the southwest monsoon to reach Kerala, on India's southwestern coast." He had nodded without really listening, the way you do at nine years old. Now the words came back whole, and he wrote them down at the top of his page in careful letters. The farmers in the region, many of them small growers, some barely more than peasants working a few flooded fields, planted when that rain arrived. If it came late, the seedlings died waiting; if it came early, the paddies filled and the season began. The date mattered because everything downstream of it mattered.

"Say the whole thing back to me," Kiera said. Landon took a breath, stood up straight like he would in front of Ms. Rajapakse's class, and began. A family waiting nearby glanced over, and a toddler clapped when he reached the part about Kerala. Kiera held up her phone and hit record. "Again, from the top," she said. "We're going to nail this."

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Glow sticks light up when bending breaks a glass vial of hydrogen peroxide inside, letting it mix with other chemicals and a dye in a reaction called chemiluminescence.
story:
Alexis sat in the back seat with his hands folded in his lap, watching the streetlights slide across the window. The dance started in twenty minutes, and his one real want was simple: to walk through the gym doors without turning around and walking back out. The car slowed at a red light, stopping on the wide grassy median beside the school road, and his mom glanced at him in the mirror. "You'll be fine," she said, which was not the same as helping. Then his phone buzzed with a message from Alanna, and he read it twice.

"Bringing glow stick bracelets for our whole group," she had written, "but one is DEAD. Cracked the whole pack testing them. Save me a slow song?" He typed back "yes" before he could talk himself out of it, and then sat there wondering about the dead one. Why would five out of six work and one not? If the light only shows up when you bend one, he thought, maybe the dead one wasn't really dead. Maybe bending it the first time hadn't done the thing bending is supposed to do. He had no way to check from the car, but he kept turning the idea over like a coin in his pocket.

The car swung into a gas station so his mom could acquire a bottle of water, and Alexis asked for two minutes and came back with a spare pack of glow sticks from the cashier, just in case. His mom raised an eyebrow but said nothing, which he took as permission.

The gym had been transformed. Streamers hung from the basketball hoops, a disco ball spun above the bleachers, and the eighth graders had built an intricate maze of balloons by the door. Alanna met him at the punch table, her arms already stacked with bracelets. She handed him the dead one. "Be my witness," she said. "It's a total dud." Alexis held it up to the lamp and studied it. The good ones he'd cracked all had that snapping feel when he bent them, like something tiny giving way inside. This one had never snapped.

"Can I try?" he asked. He gripped it in the middle and bent it slowly, listening. Nothing. He bent it the other way, pressing harder this time, and felt a faint crack, small as a knuckle pop. The bracelet flickered, then bloomed green along its whole length. Alanna grabbed his arm. "How did you know?" Behind them, Aksil had just cracked his own bracelet and was squinting at it. "Where's the light even coming from?" he asked.

"The bending breaks a little glass vial of hydrogen peroxide inside," Alexis said, "and it mixes with other chemicals and a dye. It's called chemiluminescence." Aksil cracked his bracelet again, watching it flare brighter. Alexis slid the green one onto Alanna's wrist. "Save your questions for the next slow song," she said, and pulled him toward the dance floor.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: In bear country, parks such as Yosemite count anything with a scent as 'food', so toothpaste, sunscreen and trash must go in the bear locker too.
story:
The train swayed through the foothills while Scarlett pressed her forehead against the window and counted pine trees until she lost her place. She and her parents were riding toward Yosemite for a week of camping, and her backpack sat on the seat beside her like a third passenger, stuffed with sunscreen, a toothbrush, a fresh tube of mint toothpaste, and a flashlight with batteries she had checked twice.

Across the aisle, a girl about Scarlett's age was arguing with her little brother. "We can keep the snacks in the tent," the boy insisted. "Bears can't open zippers." The girl, whose name badge from some summer camp read Zainab, rolled her eyes. "That's not how it works," she said, but she didn't sound sure, and their dad just shrugged and kept reading his magazine.

Scarlett turned around in her seat. Last summer, on the same trip with her cousin, she had left her toothpaste in the tent overnight because it wasn't food, so why would it matter? In the morning her mom had marched her back to the metal locker at the campsite and made her put it in. "In parks like this, anything with a scent counts as food," her mom had said, pointing at the locker's painted sign. Toothpaste, sunscreen, even the trash had to go in before bed. Scarlett had stood there feeling foolish, holding her little blue tube while a squirrel watched from the picnic table.

She tested the idea now, the way she had learned to in science class. If the rule counted anything with a scent, then the family across the aisle had a problem bigger than snacks. "Excuse me," she said to Zainab. "Where are you guys camping?" "Yosemite, same as you, I think," Zainab said. "There's a locker at our site." Scarlett nodded toward the brother's daypack. "It's not just snacks. Toothpaste and sunscreen and trash have to go in the bear locker too. I learned that the embarrassing way last year."

The boy groaned like this was the worst news in the world. Zainab, though, leaned forward. "Wait, so even my chapstick?" "If it smells, it goes in," Scarlett said. Zainab began digging through the daypack, pulling out chapstick, a bag of gummy worms, and a wrapper that had already started to migrate toward the bottom of the bag, sticky side out.

When the train slowed at the station, the two families ended up walking toward the same campground shuttle. Scarlett's dad struck up a conversation with Zainab's dad, and somewhere behind them the little brother was still complaining, with vigorous arm waving, about keeping his gummy worms next to his pillow. Zainab caught Scarlett's eye and mouthed, "Thank you."

That night, in the dark tent, Scarlett listened to the wind move through the trees and thought about tomorrow's hike to the waterfall, the part her dad called the climax of the whole trip. Somewhere out there, she knew, the bear locker stood shut and full, holding every scented thing on the site. She smiled, zipped her sleeping bag up to her chin, and whispered into the cold air, "Even the chapstick."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: The 4-7-8 breathing exercise, popularized by the doctor Andrew Weil, means breathing in for four counts, holding for seven and breathing out slowly for eight.
story:
Nathaniel lay in bed staring at the ceiling, listening to his own heart thump like sneakers in a dryer. Tomorrow he had the solo in the spring concert, and every time he imagined the microphone, his stomach did a slow flip. He counted sheep, then counted the glow-in-the-dark stars on his ceiling, then counted how many times his little brother snored. Forty-one. That had to be some kind of record.

Downstairs, the floorboards creaked. His dad appeared in the doorway holding a library book with a cracked spine, one titled with words Nathaniel was too tired to read. "Can't sleep either?" his dad whispered. "Your grandmother swore by something from this book. Dr. Andrew Weil, some doctor with a big reputation for this sort of thing. Want to try it?" Nathaniel groaned, but he sat up, because the alternative was lying there listening to his heartbeat until sunrise.

"Okay, it's called 4-7-8 breathing," his dad said, sitting on the edge of the bed. "Breathe in for four counts." Nathaniel inhaled, his nose whistling faintly like a tiny teakettle. His dad snorted. "Now hold it for seven." The room went very quiet. Nathaniel could hear the refrigerator humming downstairs and a car passing on the wet street, and his chest started to burn at about count five, but he hung on. "Now out, slow, for eight." Nathaniel let the air leak out of his mouth in a long, unglamorous whoosh, like a balloon losing an argument.

"That felt radical," Nathaniel said, flopping back. "In a weird way." They did it three more times. On the fourth round something odd happened: his shoulders, which had been creeping up toward his ears all evening without his noticing, sank into the mattress like they'd given up a fight. His breathing began to regulate itself, slowing down on its own, without counting. His eyelids grew heavy as wet paper towels.

"Wait," he mumbled. "Is this the trick? You get so bored counting to eight that you fall asleep out of self-defense?" His dad laughed, pulled the blanket up to Nathaniel's chin, and turned off the lamp. "Could be," he whispered from the doorway. "Try it tomorrow before the solo. If you get nervous up there, just count." In the dark, Nathaniel practiced one more time: in, four. Hold, seven. Out, eight. His last thought was of the microphone, and this time his stomach stayed perfectly still.

The next morning he found his little brother at the kitchen table, cheeks puffed out like a bullfrog. "In for four," his brother announced, "then you hold it for seven, and then the slow part is eight." Nathaniel stared. "Who taught you that?" His brother pointed at the library book, still lying open on the counter. "Dad left it in the bathroom. I read the whole page."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: The forearm has two bones: the radius, on the thumb side, and the ulna, on the little-finger side.
story:
Mya sat at the kitchen table with her arm propped on a stack of cookbooks, the new fiberglass cast ending just below her elbow. Her friend Hargun had come over with a folder of homework and a printout of her X-ray, which the radiology desk had handed over without being asked.

"Which one did you break?" Hargun asked, tapping the pale shapes on the film.

Mya held the paper up to the window light. Two long bones ran side by side from her elbow to her wrist, and one of them had a thin dark crack near the middle, like a hair stuck to the picture. She wanted to know which bone it was, and not just out of curiosity. The doctor had written a word on her discharge papers, and if she could match the word to the right bone, she could settle an argument she'd been having with herself since the hospital.

She laid her good hand flat on the table, palm up. "The one on the thumb side is the radius," she said, reading from the paper. "The one on the little-finger side is the ulna." She turned the X-ray until the hand in the picture matched her own, thumb toward her, little finger away. Then she traced along the bone that lined up with the thumb side, down from the wrist, until her fingertip stopped at the crack. The radius. That matched the word on the paper too, which made her feel briefly and cautiously optimistic that she had it right.

"Does it matter?" Hargun asked. She was already flipping the folder open, because what she actually wanted was to get the science worksheet done before dinner, and Ms. Haile had said it would incorporate diagrams, labels, and a short written section. "We have to draw the skeletal system today. I was hoping you'd help, cast and all."

"It matters to me," Mya said. She picked up a pencil with her left hand and wrote "radius" on a sticky note, pressing it onto the X-ray next to the cracked bone. Then she wrote "ulna" on a second note and reached for the other bone, but her left hand slid the paper sideways and the note stuck to the table instead.

Hargun peeled it off for her and smoothed it into place. "If you label my diagram that neatly, I'll owe you my mom's monsoon-season soup. She makes it every time it rains hard, and it's the best thing in her whole recipe book."

"Deal," Mya said. She anchored the X-ray under the cookbook stack and picked the pencil back up, resting the cast on the edge of the table where it wouldn't slide.

Outside, the first fat drops hit the window, and Hargun grinned. "See? Perfect timing."

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: At a bar or bat mitzvah, the young person often also chants the haftarah, a reading from the books of the Prophets.
story:
The paper had two headings, and John had only ever read the first one. He stood at the edge of his aunt's backyard, dodging a swarm of relatives who all wanted to pinch his cheeks and tell him how tall he'd gotten, and scrutinized the sheet his mom had printed that morning. Under "Torah portion" was the reading he'd been practicing for three weeks. Under that, in smaller type, was a second heading and a whole block of Hebrew he'd never seen before.

"Four days," his cousin Hana said, appearing beside him with a plate of kugel. "You didn't know about the second one?" She said the word "haftarah" the way you'd say "obviously," and when he stared at her she pointed at the page. "It's a reading from the books of the Prophets. At a bar or bat mitzvah you often chant that too."

"Often," John repeated, as if the word had personally betrayed him. "So it's optional?"

"It's not optional, it's just that nobody told you because everyone assumed someone else did." Hana shrugged and ate a noodle. "Classic family move."

John spent the rest of the afternoon testing a theory. He'd noticed that haftarah passages used the same chant symbols as his Torah portion, mostly, but the tune wandered differently, like the melody kept changing its mind. His theory: if he learned the symbols as a pattern, he could sing the new reading without hearing it first. He hid in the empty guest room, whispered the phrases, and got it wrong in a way that made the neighbor's dog howl. But the second attempt matched the recording on his uncle's phone, and the third was closer, and by the time the cake came out, he could stumble through half of it.

Outside, McKayla, his friend from down the street who had crashed the party for the food, held up the sheet like a referee. "The Prophets one sounds dramatic," she said. "Like a movie trailer." She cleared her throat and chanted, badly, "Thus saaaith the Lord," and John laughed so hard he had to sit down on the cooler.

"Your family is going extinct," McKayla announced, counting the last pieces of cake being divided among nine cousins. "Not enough dessert. Natural causes."

By the end of the night John could do the whole thing, wobbly but real, and he performed it once for the relatives by the fire pit while his grandmother mouthed every word along with him. His uncle's grin was infectious, and even the dog seemed to approve.

"So Saturday," Hana said, "when you chant the haftarah, you'll be fine."

John picked up the last cookie before McKayla could. "The Prophets told me to take it," he said, and took a bite.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: Parallel lines like railway tracks or the two edges of a road look as if they meet in the distance, even though they never actually meet.
story:
William pressed his pencil so hard against the paper that the lead snapped. His street looked like a wedge of cheese, flat and wrong, and the assignment was due at the end of class.

"You keep drawing the road the same width all the way back," said Olivia, leaning over from the next stool. She was already shading her own street, which curved around a corner like it had somewhere to go.

"Streets are the same width," William said. "Nobody narrows a street."

Moses spun his pencil between two fingers, agile as a drum majorette, then dropped it. "Then why does your drawing look like it's falling over?"

William stared at the paper. He thought about the footbridge over the train tracks behind his house, where he and Moses had stood last Saturday throwing pebbles into the weeds. Moses had sworn the rails got closer together near the old water tower. William had said that was crazy. "They'd have to touch," he'd argued. "The train would fall off." Moses had just pointed at the horizon, where the two shiny lines seemed to pinch together like a zipper closing.

"You were right about the tracks," William said slowly. "They look like they meet. But they don't. Not ever. The two edges of a road do the same thing. That's probably why my street looks fake. It's too even."

Olivia scooted her stool over. "So make the edges lean toward each other on the paper. Like the tracks did from the bridge."

William turned to a fresh sheet. He drew a dot in the middle and called it a vanishing point, because he'd read that phrase on Ms. Kim's poster last week and it had finally decided to mean something. Then he drew two lines from the bottom corners of the page, straight toward the dot. The street between them shrank as it went. His brain said impossible; his eyes said perfect.

"Moses, hold the ruler," he said. "I want to elaborate on this. Storefronts, lampposts, maybe a cat."

"A cat on a street?" said Moses.

"An agile cat," William said. "Leaping between rooftops."

"You just wanted to say agile again."

"Every word deserves a second chance."

Olivia laughed so hard she smudged her shading, and William helped her blend it back out with his thumb while Moses anchored the ruler for the lamppost line. The lampposts marched up the page, each one smaller than the last, all leaning toward the dot like commuters toward the last train.

Ms. Kim wandered past their table and looked for a long moment. "Where'd you two learn that?" she asked.

William pointed out the window, toward nowhere in particular, and toward a bridge beyond it. "From a train that never falls off the tracks."

Moses drew the cat anyway, mid-leap, tail like a coat hook.

activity: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
knowledge_domain: to call plays as a point guard and run a pick and roll
fact: A pick, also called a screen, is when an offensive player stands still in a defender's path so a teammate can get free.
story:
The track behind the school had six painted lanes and one basketball hoop that Mr. Ho wheeled out for the kids who got tired of running circles. Logan had been tired of running circles since September. What he wanted was to be the point guard at Friday's scrimmage, which meant he had one week to learn to call plays, a job he had discovered was harder than it looked the moment he tried it on Tuesday.

"Play twelve!" he shouted, and Matthias, who was supposed to cut left, cut right. Remington, who was supposed to get the ball, stood near the free throw line with his hands up like he was being arrested. The boy guarding Remington, a tall kid from Mr. Ho's homeroom, stayed glued to him the whole time. Every cut Remington made, the defender made too, half a step ahead, as though he'd read Logan's play call off the inside of his own eyelids.

"It's like he's attached to me," Remington said, breathing hard. "With string. Possibly wire."

Logan called a water break and sat on the infield grass, thinking. The problem wasn't Remington's cuts. The problem was something he couldn't see: the defender wasn't watching Remington at all. He was watching Logan's mouth. Every time Logan called a play, the whole defense rearranged itself like a polite audience taking their seats. His own play calls were leaking information. That was the hidden cause, and once he saw it, he couldn't stop seeing it.

He tried an experiment. "Same play," he told Remington quietly, "but this time, Matthias, you stand right in the tall kid's way. Don't move your feet. Just stand there like a mailbox."

"Why?"

"It's a pick," Logan said. "Coach calls it a screen too."

Matthias planted himself in the defender's path, arms folded, radiating a neutral expression of a boy doing absolutely nothing wrong. The tall kid slammed into him like a bird hitting a window. Remington slipped free, took Logan's pass, and laid the ball in off the backboard while the tall kid was still untangling himself and declaring, to no official, that this was unfair.

By Thursday Logan had stopped calling plays out loud entirely. He used hand signals, some of which he invented on the spot, one of which looked alarmingly like he was waving at a helicopter. When Mr. Ho wandered over from the long-jump pit to watch, Logan tried to summarize his week for him. "So I whisper now, and Matthias stands in people's way on purpose."

"A mailbox," Matthias confirmed.

Mr. Ho watched Remington roll off Matthias's shoulder, catch the pass, and score for the ninth time in a row. He nodded slowly, the way a diplomat nods at a treaty he fully intends to honor, and said, "Point guard. Friday." Then he walked back toward the long-jump pit, and Logan turned to his teammates and held up two fingers, then pointed left.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: A voice deepens during puberty because the larynx grows and the vocal folds inside it get longer and thicker, and the voice may crack while this happens.
story:
The crack happened right in the middle of Zayd's presentation on sleep, in Mr. Lombardi's health classroom. He said "the brain stays partly awake" and the word awake came out in two pieces, one low and one squeaky, like a skipping record. Somebody in the back row laughed. Zayd's ears went red and he read the rest of his note cards in a flat mumble.

Katherine had been keeping a list in the back of her notebook all semester, ever since her own body started changing and she began wondering whether the boys could feel their changes coming too. Her list had three columns: name, date, and what happened. Yassine's voice had dropped sometime over winter break, so evenly that nobody laughed. A boy in second period had cracked during the pledge. Now Zayd. She had a guess, dormant for weeks, that there was a rule underneath it: the boys whose voices broke gradually were done, and the ones who cracked were still in the middle of something. But a guess wasn't a rule unless you could test it.

At lunch she found Zayd by the vending machines. "Can you hum this?" she said, and sang a low note. He hummed it back, steady. She went up the scale, note by note, like a fire truck climbing. At the seventh note his hum snapped in half. At the eighth, it snapped again. Below that, his voice was smooth all the way down. "It's only the high ones," Katherine said, writing fast. "The low notes work fine."

"So my voice is broken," Zayd said.

"It's not broken. It's under construction."

In the health textbook's chapter on adolescence there was a diagram Katherine had skipped before, a cross-section of the throat with the larynx labeled and two lines inside it marked vocal folds. The caption read that during puberty the larynx grows and the vocal folds get longer and thicker. Katherine sat with that for a minute. Longer and thicker would make a lower sound, the way a thick guitar string sat lower than a thin one. And while the growing was happening, the high notes would fail. That fit her scale test exactly. The rule wasn't about done or unfinished; it was about size changing underneath the sound.

The next day in class, Mr. Lombardi assigned presentations again. Katherine passed Zayd a folded note: low voice, no high words. He opened it, nodded, and pushed his note cards to the bottom of the pile. When his turn came, he stood up and delivered his whole presentation in the lower register, slow and careful, and his voice held. Afterward he sat down beside her and whispered, "Did it work?"

"Every word," Katherine said, and underlined his name in her notebook.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Japan's Obon festival, held in mid-August in most regions and in July in some, honors the spirits of ancestors, who are believed to return home for a visit.
story:
The last time Simon had sat in this seat, Grandpa had been in the one beside it, complaining that the seatbelt was trying to strangle him and asking Simon to read the road signs out loud because his glasses were "on vacation." Now the seat was empty and Mom was driving them to the memorial dinner, and Simon kept turning his phone over in his hands like it might tell him something.

It did, actually. Ania was visiting relatives in Japan, and she'd sent a photo of a paper lantern glowing on a porch. "This is for my grandma," her message said. "It's Obon. Mid-August here, but July in some regions. During Obon the spirits of ancestors come home for a visit, so we light lanterns to welcome them." Simon read it three times. Grandpa had only been gone since April, and nobody had told Simon there was a schedule for goodbyes.

He decided to devise his own version, right there in the car. He dug through the door pocket and found a birthday candle left over from his sister's cupcakes, and he folded the sandwich bag from his lunch into a lopsided little lantern around it. Mom glanced over. "What are you doing back there?" "Welcoming someone," Simon said, and struck a match from the first aid kit, which he was fairly sure he wasn't allowed to touch.

The flame sputtered and went out. He tried again. It guttered sideways, whipped by the air pouring from the vent, and died again. "Mom, can you close the vent? Please?" She reached over without a word, and the flame caught and held, small and stable, cupped in his hands like something alive. That was the climax of the whole plan, and Simon hadn't even known plans had climaxes until Ms. Diallo taught it in English last year.

He held the lantern up near the empty window. "Hi, Grandpa," he said, feeling ridiculous and not caring. "We're going to dinner. There will be terrible casseroles. You'd have hated them and eaten three." Mom made a sound that was half laugh, half something else, and didn't wipe her eyes until the next red light.

"Ania says in her town it's mid-August," Simon said as they pulled into the parking lot, "but July in some regions, so it depends where you are." He looked at the little flame, then at the empty seat. "I figure we're wherever we are." He blew the candle out gently and carried it inside, cupped in both hands.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, and the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10.
story:
The folding chairs were set up in a ragged line at the edge of the community sports field, close enough to the big screen that the projected game looked almost real. Owen sat between his grandfather and his friend Romeo, a bowl of chips balanced on his knees. The grass beneath their feet was still damp from morning rain, and the field beyond the screen stretched out green and empty, fertile soil that the Parks Department had reseeded just last month.

"They didn't have anything like this in my day," Grandpa said, nodding at the screen. "I remember the very first one, you know. The Packers against the Chiefs. Nobody even knew what it would become."

Owen sat up straighter. "You remember the first one? That was forever ago."

"January fifteenth, 1967," Grandpa said, tapping the arm of his chair. "Green Bay won it going away. Thirty-five to ten."

Romeo leaned over. "No way. Nobody remembers a score from that long ago. My dad can't even remember what he had for breakfast."

"I remember it because we all crowded into Al's Barbershop to watch," Grandpa said. "Half the town in one room."

Owen pulled out his phone and turned it sideways so Romeo could see the screen. "My grandpa says the first one was Packers versus Chiefs, January fifteenth, 1967, and the Packers won thirty-five to ten," he said quietly, typing. Romeo watched over his shoulder, bouncing one knee.

The search results loaded. Owen scrolled once, then twice, and stopped. "It's all here. Every part of it. The date, the score, the teams." He held the phone low so only Romeo could see. "He got it exactly right. He really does remember it."

"Old people remember the important stuff," Romeo said. "It's the breakfast they lose."

Owen laughed, then looked up at his grandfather, who was squinting at the screen where the teams were lining up for the second half. "Grandpa, I checked. You were right. Every number."

"Of course I was right," Grandpa said, but his shoulders straightened and he smiled at the field. "You don't forget a day like that."

The crowd around them groaned as a pass fell incomplete, and somebody's little sister started crying near the snack table. A woman hurried over to reassure her, patting her back and offering popcorn until the tears stopped. The commentator's voice boomed out over the grass, saying something about adrenaline, the hormone that surges in a close game, and Owen felt a little of it himself as the score stayed tight.

Fourth quarter, two minutes left, his team down by four. Romeo grabbed Owen's sleeve without taking his eyes off the screen. Grandpa folded his hands in his lap, calm as anything, as though he had watched enough football in his life to know exactly how this one would end.

The quarterback dropped back, planted his feet, and let the ball fly.
